Learning Objectives

Evaluate and diagnose patients in whom a scapular fracture is suspected.

The scapula connects the chest wall to the upper limb and provides a stable base for the upper
extremity to work against.
Scapular fractures typically result from high-energy mechanisms of injury.
Other injuries commonly are associated with scapular fractures; therefore, patients require
thorough evaluation.

Overview
The scapula is an important connection between the axial skeleton and the upper
extremity. It serves as the origin or insertion for 18 different muscles and articulates via
the acromioclavicular joint, glenohumeral joint, and scapulothoracic articulation. Given
the support of the surrounding soft tissues and relative mobility of the scapula, fractures
tend to result from high-energy mechanisms of injury, such as motor vehicle or
motorcycle collisions or falls from a height. Typically these are high-energy injuries;
therefore, patients with a scapular fracture frequently have associated injuries that may
be life- or limb-threatening and require a careful and thorough evaluation.
Epidemiology
Scapular fractures account for 3% to 5% of shoulder girdle injuries and less than 1% of all
fractures.
Scapular fractures tend to result from high-energy events, such as motor vehicle or motorcycle
collisions, which account for approximately 90% of all fractures; however, a bimodal age
distribution is beginning to develop, with an increase in fragility fractures in the elderly.
Scapular fractures are associated with a hemothorax or pneumothorax in 80% of patients, an
ipsilateral extremity injury in 50% of patients, a head injury in 15% of patients, a cervical injury
in 15% of patients, and neurovascular injury in 10% patients.
Scapular fractures are missed or diagnosis is delayed in as many as 15% of patients with
multiple injuries.

Scapular fractures are rare, making up only 1% of all fractures and 3% to 5% of injuries
of the shoulder girdle. Given the relatively protected location of the scapula, fractures
tend to result from high-energy mechanisms of injury, such as motor vehicle collisions.1
However, as the population continues to age, an increasing bimodal distribution of
scapular fractures has been observed, with the rate of fractures from ground-level falls
increasing from 10.6% in 2002 to 17.8% in 2012.2
Because of the high-energy mechanisms of injury, patients with a scapular fracture
frequently have associated injuries. A recent review of the National Trauma Database
showed that patients with a scapular fractures had a mean Injury Severity Score of 20.1.2
The most frequently associated injuries include hemothorax or pneumothorax (as high
as 80%), rib fractures (63%), vertebral fractures (40.3%), and ipsilateral extremity injuries
(50%).2,3 Frequently, associated head trauma or injuries to nearby neurovascular
structures, including the brachial plexus or axillary artery, are present. Because of the
frequently associated distracting injuries, scapular fractures may be missed and/or
diagnosis delayed in as many as 15% of patients.4
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The scapula consists of the body, spine, acromion, glenoid, and coracoid processes.
The scapula is the origin or insertion for 18 muscles.

Osteology
To diagnose and manage scapular fractures, surgeons must understand the complex
anatomy of the scapula and the shoulder girdle. Knowledge of the movements of the
scapula relative to the chest wall is important. The scapula is composed of the body and
four processes: the scapular spine, acromion, coracoid, and glenoid (Figure 1).
The body of the scapula begins to ossify during the eighth week of gestation. It
articulates with the posterior chest wall. One-third of shoulder motion occurs at the

scapulothoracic articulation, and six primary movements of the scapula against the chest
occur: elevation, depression, upward rotation, downward rotation, protraction, and
retraction. Injuries to the scapula may lead to disruption of these normal movements,
abnormal scapular mechanics, and upper extremity dysfunction.
The scapular spine projects posteriorly from the scapular body and separates the
supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae. The spine begins at the medial border of the
scapula and extends laterally until it meets the acromion and the glenoid processes at
the spinoglenoid notch. The spinoglenoid notch is a potential site of suprascapular nerve
tethering or compression.
The acromion extends laterally from the end of the scapular spine before turning
anteriorly to cover the humeral head. The acromion arises from three ossification
centers: the meta-acromion develops into the posterior acromion, the meso-acromion
develops into the midportion of the acromion, and the pre-acromion develops into the
anterior acromial tip.5 These structures typically fuse together and to the scapular spine
by age 18 years; however, ossification centers may be observed as late as age 25 years.6
Patients have an os acromiale if any of these ossification centers persist into adulthood.
Although most patients with an os acromiale are asymptomatic and do not require
treatment,7 an acute injury may destabilize a previously asymptomatic os acromiale and
make it painful.
The coracoid process extends superiorly from the glenoid neck before turning anteriorly
and laterally. The coracoid tip is the origin of the coracobrachialis and the short head of
the biceps (together referred to as the conjoint tendon or strap muscles), the insertion of
the pectoralis minor, and the attachment site of the coracoacromial ligament. The
coracoclavicular ligaments (conoid and trapezoid ligaments) attach more proximally on
the coracoid.
The glenoid is an intra-articular structure composed of the glenoid rim and the glenoid
fossa, which extends laterally from the scapular body and neck and articulates with the
humeral head as the glenohumeral joint. The glenoid is pear-shaped and shallow,
making the glenohumeral joint inherently unstable. The surrounding labrum deepens
the glenoid fossa by as much as 50%, allowing for enhanced glenohumeral stability. Wide

The scapula receives its blood supply from four main vessels, two sets of vessels that
anastomose with each other.
The suprascapular artery and the circumflex scapular artery

The circumflex scapular artery is at risk during a posterior approach to the scapula.

Vascular Anatomy
The scapula has a blood supply composed of four main blood vessels. These can be
thought of as two sets of vessels that anastomose with each other on the medial or
lateral aspects of the scapula. The suprascapular artery courses superficial to the
transverse scapular ligament and courses inferolaterally through the spinoglenoid notch
and into the infraspinatus fossa. The circumflex scapular artery courses through the
triangular space and around the lateral border of the scapula to the infraspinatus fossa,
the location at which it anastomoses with the suprascapular artery. The circumflex
scapular artery (specifically its ascending branch) is the vessel most at risk during a
posterior approach to the scapula. The medial scapular body is perfused by the
anastomosis between the thoracodorsal artery and the dorsal scapular artery.
Neural Anatomy
The suprascapular nerve travels deep to the transverse scapular ligament through the
spinoglenoid notch.
The axillary nerve travels in proximity to the inferior glenoid neck.
The brachial plexus is at risk of injury with scapulothoracic dissociation.

Neural Anatomy
Important nervous structures are in proximity to the scapula. The suprascapular nerve
arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus and courses through the
suprascapular notch, deep to the transverse ligament, into the supraspinatus fossa. The
nerve then courses inferolaterally through the spinoglenoid notch and into the
infraspinatus fossa (Figure 2).

Superior Shoulder Suspensory Complex
The superior shoulder suspensory complex (SSSC) is shown in Figure 5.
The SSSC consists of the glenoid, coracoid process, distal clavicle, acromion, and ligamentous
structures of the acromioclavicular joint and coracoclavicular ligaments.
It plays an important role in shoulder stability and biomechanics.
The coracoacromial ligament was excluded from the original description of the SSSC but
plays an important stabilizing role in double disruption injuries.


Superior Shoulder Suspensory Complex
The SSSC is a ring of bony and soft-tissue structures that helps maintain a stable
relationship between the upper extremity, scapula, and axial skeleton. As originally
described, the SSSC is composed of the glenoid, coracoid, coracoclavicular ligaments,
distal clavicle, acromioclavicular joint, and acromion. This ring of tissue is supported by
two bony struts medially, the middle clavicle and the scapular body/spine. Injuries to one
of these structures, called a single disruption of the SSSC, do not disrupt the overall
integrity of the ring. Injuries to two of the structures, or of the medial bony struts, are
termed double disruptions of the SSSC and can destabilize the complex and the upper
extremity.10 The coracoacromial ligament was excluded from the original description of
the SSSC; however, biomechanical studies have shown that it plays an important

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Mechanisms of injury
A lateral to medial force causes scapular body, neck, and glenoid fractures.
An axial load via the outstretched upper extremity can cause scapular neck and glenoid
fractures.
A glenohumeral dislocation can cause anterior (bony Bankart) or posterior (reverse bony
Bankart) glenoid fractures.
A scapulothoracic dissociation is a lateral displacement of the scapula associated with severe
soft-tissue injury and a brachial plexus and vascular injury of the extremity.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Scapular fractures most commonly result from a lateral-to-medial force applied to the
scapula. Similarly, indirect forces, such as an axial load onto an outstretched upper
extremity, can produce a lateral-to-medial force on the scapula via the humeral head
and can lead to scapular neck and glenoid fractures. A recent review showed that motor
vehicle collisions, motorcycle crashes, and falls were responsible for 27.8%, 24.6%, and
17.8% of scapular fractures, respectively.2
A subset of glenoid fractures may be associated with glenohumeral instability and
dislocation. Specifically, anterior shoulder dislocations may lead to anteroinferior glenoid
fractures (bony Bankart), and posterior shoulder dislocations may lead to posteroinferior
glenoid fractures (reverse bony Bankart).
Although typically not associated with a scapular fracture, a scapulothoracic dissociation
may be a devastating injury. Scapulothoracic dissociation consists of a traumatic
dissociation of the scapula and upper extremity from the chest wall. This results from a

injury that ranges from traction neuropraxia to complete avulsion of the brachial
plexus.13
Associated Injuries
Scapular fractures should be thought of as a surrogate for high-energy trauma.
Associated injuries may be nearby or distant, and patients require a thorough tertiary
examination to identify all injuries present.
Patients with scapular fractures have a mean of 3.9 additional injuries.14

Associated Injuries
Scapular fractures require a considerable traumatic force, and the authors of this lesson
recommend viewing these injuries as surrogates to identify patients who require a
thorough tertiary examination. The most frequently associated injuries include
hemothorax or pneumothorax (as high as 80%), rib fractures (63%), vertebral fractures
(40.3%), and ipsilateral extremity injuries (50%).2,3 Patients also may sustain injuries to
the brachial plexus, head trauma, distant osseous injuries, and great vessel injuries.15,16
Case reports of associated compartment syndromes or quadrilateral space syndromes
have been noted.17,18 Although scapular fractures are associated with other substantial
injuries and increased Injury Severity Scores, they are not associated with an increased
risk of mortality.2,19,20
Injury Classification
Classification is based on the location of the fracture on the scapula.

Injury Classification
Multiple classification systems have been described for scapular fractures. An
understanding of the clinical relevance of each classification system and how it helps
determine appropriate management and expected outcomes is more important that
memorizing multiple classification system.
Some classification system focus specifically on fractures of the processes of the scapula.
The Ogawa classification of coracoid fractures differentiates fractures based on whether
the fracture is proximal or distal to the coracoclavicular ligaments.21 If present with
other injuries in the SSSC, fractures that are proximal to the coracoclavicular ligaments
represent a destabilizing injury, whereas those distal to the coracoclavicular ligaments
may maintain stability of the shoulder girdle. The Kuhn classification of acromial
fractures is based on fracture displacement and impingement on the subacromial
space.22 For patients with nondisplaced fractures or displaced fractures that do not
compromise the subacromial space, nonsurgical management often is successful. If the
subacromial space is decreased because of a displaced fracture, mechanical
impingement limits shoulder function and surgical management is warranted. More
recently, Levy et al23 added an acromial classification system based on the location of
the fracture, which has implications for management, especially in the setting of reverse
shoulder arthroplasty.

Other classification systems encompass a wider range of scapular fractures, such as the
Euler and Ideberg/Mayo classification systems;24,25 however, some fracture patterns
cannot be classified with these systems. Subsequently, the Orthopaedic Trauma
Association/AO Foundation described a new classification system designed to be reliable
and reproducible and to help guide future clinical studies.26,27 Although studies are
necessary to determine how this new classification system relates to treatment decisions
and clinical outcomes, it is associated with a higher interrater and intra-rater reliability
than the previously established classification systems.28
Injuries to the SSSC can be described based on the number of areas in which the
stabilizing circle has been disrupted. Although the importance of double disruptions of
the SSSC and the potential for an unstable floating shoulder was recognized initially,
more recent literature has described triple and quadruple disruptions.29 These injuries
are associated with higher rates of associated injuries and nerve injuries.
The most commonly used classification system for scapulothoracic dissociation is the
Zelle classification system.30 This classification system is based on the degree of vascular
and neurologic involvement and is most useful as a prognostic tool. Type 1 to type 3
scapulothoracic dissociations have varying degrees of vascular and neurologic
involvement; however, patients with complete brachial plexus avulsions (type 4) typically
have poor outcomes and little chance of neurologic recovery (Table 3).

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients typically present with high-energy, blunt trauma to the shoulder.
A history that includes a baseline level of function and the patient’s occupation, hobbies, and
hand dominance should be obtained.

Patient History
The clinical evaluation of patients with a scapular fracture begins with a thorough
history. A thorough understanding of the patient’s baseline functional status,
occupation, hobbies, comorbidities, hand dominance, and goals of treatment is
necessary to guide treatment decisions. The mechanism of injury typically is high-energy
blunt trauma; however, is an increasing bimodal distribution is noted as more scapular
fractures are identified in geriatric patients after lower energy falls. Given the high rate
of associated injuries, patients should be questioned about chest pain, neck and back
pain, difficulty breathing, and paresthesias and weakness of the ipsilateral extremity.
Physical Examination
The incidence of injuries associated with scapular and glenoid fractures is high (90%).
Identifying the mechanism of injury is helpful in determining other injuries.
The skin should be examined for abrasions or open wounds.
A thorough neurovascular examination of the affected extremity must be performed.

Physical Examination

Given the high-energy mechanisms of injury typically associated with scapular fractures,
Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol should be followed. Subsequently, a
comprehensive orthopaedic examination should be performed. All patients with a
scapular fracture require not only a thorough physical examination of the involved
extremity but also a systematic tertiary examination for possible associated injuries.
Patients often hold the injured extremity in adduction and guard against participation in
a physical examination because of pain. Visual inspection should evaluate for swelling,
ecchymosis, abrasions, and open wounds; however, the amount of ecchymosis often is
less than expected because of the robust soft-tissue envelope surrounding the scapula.
Intact skin should not be thought of as a marker of lesser trauma because patients with
scapulothoracic dissociation often have intact skin but still have devastating injuries.
A neurovascular examination of the involved extremity should be performed. Special
attention should be given to peripheral pulses, hand temperature, and the appearance
of the limb because limb-threatening ischemia has been reported to occur in 10% of
patients with scapulothoracic dissociation.30 If patients are able to participate in a
neurologic examination, the entirety of the brachial plexus should be examined. Findings
such as ptosis, anhidrosis, and miosis suggest Horner syndrome and are a marker of a
preganglionic nerve injury, which portends a poorer prognosis for patients with
scapulothoracic dissociation.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
True AP (Grashey), trans-scapular (Y), and axillary views of the proximal humerus should be
obtained.
Obtaining quality radiographs often is difficult secondary to patient discomfort and lack of
radiographic protocols.
Radiographic parameters include intra-articular step-off, lateral border offset (medialization),
glenopolar angle (angle on a true AP view of the glenoid surface relative to the inferior wing),
and angulation (observed on a trans-scapular view).

Radiography
All patients in whom a scapular fracture is suspected require a complete imaging series,
including true AP (Grashey), scapular Y, and axillary views. Although obtaining high-
quality radiographs in a trauma patient may be difficult because of patient discomfort,
these baseline images are critical because they help guide management and patients are
followed radiographically to monitor healing in the outpatient setting.

Multiple radiographic parameters help guide decision making for scapular fractures.
Glenoid fractures should be evaluated for step-off of the articular surface. Scapular neck
and body fractures may disrupt the lateral border of the scapula or the angle of the
glenoid relative to the inferior pole (glenopolar angle). Fractures that split the scapula
into superior and inferior fragments may allow for angulation of the fragments relative

Coracoid Fractures
The need for surgical fixation of coracoid fractures is based on the stability of the
coracoid fragments, extension into the scapular body or glenoid, and the integrity of the
SSSC.
Fractures of the coracoid tip typically are avulsion injuries from the pull of the conjoint
tendon and often lead to considerable displacement. Nonsurgical management typically
is the preferred treatment option for coracoid avulsions because the SSSC is not
disrupted; however, some studies recommend fixation for athletes and heavy
laborers.35 Occasionally, the continued pull of the tendons on the tip fragment may lead
to a nonunion and irritation of the surrounding soft tissues, requiring late fixation or
excision with soft-tissue repair.36
Fractures of the coracoid base result from direct trauma or from the force of a
dislocating humeral head.37 Isolated coracoid fractures often are minimally displaced
because of the stabilizing effect of the intact coracoclavicular and coracoacromial
ligaments on the distal fragment; however, surgical fixation may be necessary in
fractures displaced more than 1 cm or if the fracture extends into the upper scapula or
glenoid fossa.38
The combination of a coracoid fracture and a second disruption of the SSSC may
represent a double disruption of the complex. The most common structure injured along
with a coracoid fracture is the acromioclavicular joint, and management should begin
with assessment of the stability of the SSSC.39 If the complex is unstable, surgical
management to address the acromioclavicular joint alone may be sufficient to reduce
the coracoid fracture.40 If still displaced, the coracoid also should be reduced and fixed.

Glenoid Fractures
Most glenoid fractures are minimally displaced and can be managed nonsurgically. If
fractures are displaced, the congruity of the glenoid articular surface is disrupted,
leading to an increased risk of posttraumatic arthritis and, if the glenoid fragment is
large enough, instability of the glenohumeral joint. No strict indications for surgical
management exist based on articular step-off, with various studies recommending step-
off from 2 to 10 mm; however, a cutoff of 4 mm frequently is used.25,33,42 Fractures
involving a large enough portion of the glenoid may allow the humeral head to subluxate
in the direction of the fracture. Although the exact percentage of glenoid that needs to
be involved to allow for subluxation is not well defined, if subluxation is present, the
fracture should be reduced and fixed to restore the bony support of the glenohumeral
joint.25 Beyond fracture characteristics, the surgeon also must consider the patient’s
baseline functional status, medical comorbidities, and goals of treatment if surgical
management is pursued. For elderly patients and/or those with lower functional
demands, a larger intra-articular gap may be tolerated; in younger, higher demand
patients with a smaller articular step-off, consideration of surgical management may be
beneficial.

Scapular Body Fractures
A scapular body fracture is the most common type of scapular fracture, accounting for
more than 50% of scapular fractures.43 Although more than 90% of scapular body
fractures can be managed nonsurgically, a growing body of literature focuses on surgical
management and indications for scapular fractures. The indications for surgical fixation
are based on fracture displacement and its potential effect on muscle length and
function around the shoulder girdle, with several series showing that fractures healing
with residual displacement may lead to persistent pain and decreased function.44,45
Specifically, disruption of scapular length and angulation of the glenoid or scapular body
may contribute to disability after scapular body fracture.
Scapular length is assessed via medial-lateral translation of the glenoid relative to the
lateral border of the scapula (Figure 8, C), with medialization of more than 20 mm being
an indication for fixation. Angulation of the glenoid relative to the scapular body may
occur in patients with a body fracture that extends into the neck. Glenoid angulation is
assessed via the glenopolar angle, measured as the angle between the inferior angle of
the scapula, the superior aspect of the glenoid, and the inferior aspect of the glenoid. A
normal glenopolar angle ranges from 35° to 45°46 (Figure 8, A). A smaller glenopolar
angle (relative inferior tilting of the glenoid) is negatively correlated with functional
outcomes; poorer outcomes are associated with a glenopolar angle less than 20°.47
Anterior or posterior angulation of the scapular body is another deformity that may
disrupt the function of the shoulder girdle, with angulation of more than 45° most
commonly cited as the threshold for surgical fixation48 (Figure 8, B). Lastly, displaced
fractures of the scapular body that involve additional disruptions of the SSSC warrant
surgical stabilization.

The SSSC, as described by Goss,10 is a bony and soft-tissue ring that is responsible for
maintaining the normal stable relationship between the upper extremity and the axial
skeleton.10 As the only bony connection between the axial skeleton and the upper
extremity, the clavicle serves as one of the bony struts medially, whereas the scapular
body and spine serve as the second. The SSSC is the complex that links the clavicle and
scapula, creating a stable platform on which the glenohumeral joint can rotate and
function. Although disruptions in a single location of the SSSC are inherently stable,
injuries to multiple structures within the stabilizing ring may destabilize the complex,
leading to healing problems and/or functional impairment of the shoulder.49
Recognition that not all double disruptions of the SSSC are unstable is key. In the classic
floating shoulder, a concomitant glenoid neck and midshaft clavicle fracture, an intact
coracoacromial ligament provides a direct connection between the medial and lateral
scapula fragments and maintains as much as 70% of the stability of the SSSC;11 however,
because it is difficult to assess ligamentous integrity on plain radiographs or CT scans,
displacement often is used as a proxy for ligamentous disruption. Multiple series have
shown good-to-excellent outcomes with nonsurgical management of minimally
displaced scapular neck and midshaft clavicle fractures.50,51 In patients with more
considerable displacement or additional disruptions of the SSSC, surgical stabilization of
the complex should be pursued.29,52,53

given the robust surrounding soft tissues, and union rates as high as 100% have been
reported.42
Rehabilitation
Patients who undergo nonsurgical treatment of a scapular or glenoid fractures typically are
immobilized in a sling or shoulder immobilizer and perform gentle Codman exercises for 2
weeks. These patients are advanced to full active and passive range of motion after 3 weeks,
with resistive activities initiated 6 weeks postinjury.
For surgically managed scapular and glenoid fractures, immediate, full active and passive
range of motion typically is prescribed for the first 4 weeks; a gradual strengthening program
is then initiated.
Anterior approaches that involve subscapularis takedown require limiting shoulder external
rotation for 6 weeks.

Rehabilitation
A sling is used initially for patient comfort; however, as the fracture consolidates and
pain subsides, the patient may increase use of the arm. Symptoms should be managed
with ice, anti-inflammatories, and sling immobilization. Patients often find sleeping in a
recliner rather than supine or in a recumbent position to be helpful. Elbow, wrist, and
hand exercises should be initiated as soon as comfort allows to prevent stiffness.
Patients with a scapular fracture managed nonsurgically should be observed closely for
the first 2 to 3 weeks to assess for progressive deformity and fracture displacement.61
Physical therapy may be helpful initially to focus on maintaining shoulder range of
motion and to prevent stiffness, and later to progressively strengthen the involved

After surgical fixation of scapular fractures, patients should remain non–weight-bearing;
however, if the surgeon feels enough stability is present in the surgical construct, then
active and passive range of shoulder motion should begin immediately. Initiating motion
may help prevent postoperative stiffness and avoid the need for a manipulation or soft-
tissue release if patients are unable to regain full range.58 Typically, by 4 to 5 weeks
postoperatively, enough early healing is present for the patient to begin light
strengthening, with progressive increases in strengthening over the second and third
postoperative month. By 3 to 4 months postoperatively, all restrictions generally are
removed.48
In patients with an anterior glenoid fracture or other fracture that requires dissection
deep to the subscapularis, rehabilitation must be modified to allow for appropriate
subscapularis healing. If the subscapularis muscle is split but left in continuity, then no
change to the rehabilitation protocol is necessary; however, if the subscapularis is taken
down and repaired, then patients should be advised to limit active internal rotation and
passive external rotation for 6 weeks postoperatively to allow for subscapularis healing.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Suprascapular nerve injury is associated with scapular neck fractures that involve the
spinoglenoid and suprascapular notches. Preoperative electromyography is recommended if
the fracture involves the spinoglenoid notch and more than 2 weeks have elapsed since injury.
Deformity and dysfunction are related. Restoration of length, alignment, rotation, and articular
congruity are important treatment principles.
